title: Christmas on $20 in 1951: 12 Grandma Tricks That Still Work Today

scenes.text: Sweetheart, every year your mother tells me Christmas costs too much. The gifts, the lights, the wrapping paper you throw away in ten minutes. And every year I tell her the same thing. In nineteen fifty-one, my mother made the most beautiful Christmas I ever had, for four people and Grandma Pearl, with about twenty dollars. And almost every trick she used, you can still use today.
scenes.caption: TWENTY DOLLARS

scenes.text: So tonight I'm going to give you twelve of them. Twelve of my mother's Christmas tricks. I'll tell you how we did it in nineteen fifty-one, and exactly how you can do it this year, in your own kitchen. Get a pencil, honey. Your mother will want this list.
scenes.caption: TWELVE TRICKS

scenes.text: Trick number one. Start in January. My mother kept a Mason jar on the top shelf of the pantry, and every Friday when my father brought home his pay, a quarter went into the jar. Sometimes fifty cents. By December there was enough for the whole of Christmas, and not one penny of it was borrowed. Nobody we knew bought Christmas on credit.
scenes.caption: A QUARTER EVERY FRIDAY

scenes.text: Today, sweetheart, do the same thing. Pick a jar or a little savings account, and put in the same amount every single week, starting in January. Even five dollars a week is two hundred and sixty dollars by December. And when you shop, you only spend what's in the jar. When it's empty, Christmas is bought.
scenes.query: vintage glass jar savings money table
scenes.caption: WHEN IT'S EMPTY

scenes.text: Trick number two. Buy the tree late. Christmas trees in nineteen fifty-one cost about a dollar or two at the lot by the gas station. But on the twenty-second or twenty-third of December, the man wanted to go home, and my father would offer him fifty cents for the one with the bare side. You just turn the bare side to the wall. Nobody ever knows.
scenes.query: 1950s Christmas tree lot man buying tree
scenes.caption: TURN IT TO THE WALL

scenes.text: My tip for a real tree, sweetheart. When you get it home, saw an inch off the bottom of the trunk, right away, and stand it in a bucket of water in the garage overnight before you bring it in. Keep it far from the radiator or the heater, and check the water every single morning. Our tree in nineteen fifty-one drank a quart a day, and it never dropped a needle until New Year's.
scenes.query: 1950s father carrying Christmas tree into house
scenes.caption: SAW AN INCH OFF

scenes.text: Trick number three. Popcorn and cranberry garlands. My mother popped a big pot of popcorn on the stove the day before, and left it out overnight, because fresh popcorn crumbles but day-old popcorn holds. Then Danny and I sat at the kitchen table with a needle and heavy thread, three pieces of popcorn and one cranberry, over and over, for hours. And yes, we ate half of it.
scenes.caption: THREE AND ONE

scenes.text: Here's my tip, sweetheart. Use upholstery thread or dental floss, it doesn't break. Wet the end of the needle. Make them about six feet long, and drape them on the tree last, after the lights. And when Christmas is over, take them outside and hang them on a bush for the birds. That's what we did. The cardinals loved Christmas almost as much as we did.
scenes.query: red cardinal bird winter snow bush
scenes.caption: FOR THE BIRDS

scenes.text: Trick number four. Paper chains. Every school child in America made them. Strips of colored paper, an inch wide and six inches long, looped and pasted with flour paste. Flour and water, that's all paste was in our house. We hung them in every doorway, and Grandma Pearl counted the loops to tell us how many days until Christmas. Tear off one loop every morning.
scenes.caption: FLOUR PASTE

scenes.text: Today you can make them from old magazines, wrapping paper scraps or the children's drawings, with a stapler instead of flour paste. Make one loop for every day from the first of December, and write something on the inside of each loop. A Bible verse, a joke, or a little job. Call Grandma. Bake cookies. Hug your brother. My mother did that in nineteen fifty-three, and I've done it ever since.
scenes.query: colorful paper chain garland children doorway
scenes.caption: ONE LOOP A DAY

scenes.text: Trick number five, and this one is my favorite. Orange pomanders. You take an orange and push whole cloves into it, all over, so close they almost touch. My mother rolled them in cinnamon and set them in a dish in the front room, and the whole house smelled like Christmas from Thanksgiving to New Year's. No candles, no sprays. Just an orange and a box of cloves.
scenes.caption: AN ORANGE AND A BOX OF CLOVES

scenes.text: My tip. Use a toothpick to make the holes first, or your thumbs will be sore for a week. Do it in early December so they have time to dry. And tie a red ribbon around them and hang them on the tree, or in a closet. They last for years, sweetheart. I still have one my mother made in nineteen sixty. It's hard as a rock and it still smells like her.
scenes.caption: IT STILL SMELLS LIKE HER

scenes.text: Trick number six. Snow on the windows. In the fifties, mothers mixed Bon Ami powder cleanser with a little water into a paste and painted it on the inside of the windows with a sponge, through a paper stencil. A star, a bell, a candle. When it dried, it looked like frost. And after Christmas, you wiped it off and the windows were cleaner than before. My mother liked that part best.
scenes.caption: BON AMI

scenes.text: Today you can do the same thing with a little bar soap mixed with water, or with the spray snow from the store if you like. Cut a stencil out of a cereal box. Do it with the children on a Saturday. The point isn't the decoration, sweetheart. The point is the Saturday.
scenes.caption: THE POINT IS THE SATURDAY

scenes.text: Trick number seven. Cookies are presents. My mother baked for two weeks before Christmas, and the cookies went in tins to the mailman, the milkman, the teacher, the minister, the widow across the street. That was how you said thank you. And every lady on Elm Street did the same, so in the end everybody's tins went around the street and came back full of somebody else's cookies.
scenes.caption: THE TINS WENT AROUND

scenes.text: Here's my mother's sugar cookie, sweetheart, write it down. One cup of butter, soft. One cup of sugar. One egg. A teaspoon of vanilla. Two and a half cups of flour and a teaspoon of baking powder. Mix it, wrap it in wax paper, and put it in the icebox overnight. That's the secret, the night in the cold. Roll it out, cut your stars, and bake at three seventy-five for about eight minutes, until the edges just turn gold.
scenes.query: rolling cookie dough star cutters kitchen
scenes.caption: THE NIGHT IN THE COLD

scenes.text: And here's how you keep them, honey. Soft cookies and crisp cookies never go in the same tin, or the crisp ones go soft. My mother put a slice of bread in the tin with the soft ones to keep them fresh, and changed it every few days. And she always hid one tin behind the flour in the pantry for Christmas Eve, because by the twentieth, my father and Danny had found all the others.
scenes.query: vintage cookie tins pantry shelf Christmas
scenes.caption: A SLICE OF BREAD IN THE TIN

scenes.text: Trick number eight. Never throw away wrapping paper. Grandma Pearl took every piece off so carefully you'd think it was a bomb, then she ironed it flat with a cool iron and folded it in the cedar chest for next year. Same with the ribbons. Some of our paper was on its fourth Christmas. We teased her about it. I do it myself now.
scenes.caption: SHE IRONED IT

scenes.text: And when there wasn't any paper, we used the Sunday funnies. Dick Tracy and Blondie and Little Orphan Annie, all wrapped around a present, with red yarn and a sprig of pine from the tree. Or brown paper from the butcher, with a potato stamp. You cut a star into half a potato, dip it in paint, and stamp it all over. Children love it. And it costs nothing.
scenes.caption: THE SUNDAY FUNNIES

scenes.text: Trick number nine. Make one gift with your own hands. That year I knitted my father a pair of mittens. Grandma Pearl taught me. One thumb was longer than the other, and the left one had a hole I didn't know about. He wore them every winter until nineteen sixty, at the plant, and when they fell apart, he kept them in his dresser drawer. I found them there when he died.
scenes.caption: ONE THUMB WAS LONGER

scenes.text: Today it can be anything, sweetheart. A jar of your own cookies with a ribbon. A photograph in a frame. A little book of coupons for your mother, one breakfast in bed, one week of dishes, one hour of no arguing. Your great-grandfather Walter got one of those from Danny in nineteen fifty-three. He said it was the best present he ever got. He used the no-arguing coupon the same night.
scenes.caption: ONE HOUR OF NO ARGUING

scenes.text: Trick number ten. An orange in the toe. Every stocking in our house had an orange down in the toe, and a handful of nuts in their shells, and a candy cane, and one little thing. A yo-yo. A box of crayons. A pair of socks. Grandma Pearl started it, because in the Depression an orange in December was a luxury. To me it still is.
scenes.query: Christmas stocking orange nuts candy cane
scenes.caption: AN ORANGE IN THE TOE

scenes.text: My tip, honey. Fill the stockings with small, useful, happy things. A toothbrush in a fun color. Socks. A little flashlight. Some chocolate. And always the orange. It's the cheapest thing in the stocking, and it's the one your children will remember when they're old.
scenes.query: orange fruit Christmas morning fireplace stockings
scenes.caption: THE ONE THEY'LL REMEMBER

scenes.text: Trick number eleven. Music is free. In nineteen fifty-one, the radio played Christmas songs all December. Gene Autry singing Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, which was brand new then, and Frosty the Snowman, newer still. And Bing Crosby, of course, White Christmas, every hour. We had no money for records, so we sang around the upright piano at Grandma Pearl's. Every night of Advent, after supper.
scenes.caption: AROUND THE PIANO

scenes.text: Do that, sweetheart. One night, turn off every screen in the house, put on the old songs, and sing. Badly, it doesn't matter. Our Danny sang so off-key that the dog left the room. That's the memory I have of Christmas, more than any present. Danny singing, and the dog leaving the room.
scenes.caption: THE DOG LEFT THE ROOM

scenes.text: And trick number twelve, the most important one. Every Christmas, my mother picked one family at church who was having a hard year. A father out of work, a mother who was sick. And without telling anyone, she'd leave a box on their porch on Christmas Eve. A chicken, a pie, some oranges, and something for each child. We never signed it. She said if you sign it, it's not a gift.
scenes.caption: IF YOU SIGN IT

scenes.text: Danny and I were the ones who ran it up to the porch and rang the bell and ran. We hid behind the hedge to watch the door open. That was the best part of Christmas for me, sweetheart. Better than any present I ever got. And you can do it this year. It doesn't take twenty dollars. It just takes one porch.
scenes.query: children running snowy street night Christmas lights
scenes.caption: IT JUST TAKES ONE PORCH

scenes.text: So there they are. Twelve tricks from nineteen fifty-one. The jar, the late tree, the popcorn, the paper chains, the pomanders, the window snow, the cookies, the wrapping, the homemade gift, the orange in the toe, the music, and the box on somebody's porch. Tomorrow night I'll tell you another Christmas, and another tip. Every day until Christmas, sweetheart.
scenes.caption: EVERY DAY UNTIL CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: And tell me in the comments. What was the one thing your mother always did at Christmas that you still do? I'll read every single one. Goodnight, sweetheart. Grandma Ruth will be right here tomorrow.
scenes.query: vintage Christmas living room fireplace stockings
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOUR MOTHER DO?
